name: Molecular Diagnostics
description: Iran’s molecular-diagnostics infrastructure includes laboratories using nucleic-acid tests to identify infectious pathogens. Its COVID-19 response illustrates both the expansion of testing networks and the importance of assay validation, staff training, and external quality assessment.

seo.title: Molecular Diagnostics in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s molecular-testing networks, the COVID-19 laboratory response, and the evidence needed to assess diagnostic quality and access.

content.heading: A diagnostic test is also a system
content.content:
Molecular diagnostics identifies biological targets through their genetic material. In Iran’s COVID-19 response, polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, became a central laboratory method for detecting the virus responsible for the disease. Reverse-transcription PCR first converts viral RNA into DNA before amplification. The national laboratory account describes evaluating both RNA-extraction kits and real-time PCR assays: obtaining a reliable result depended on the preparation stage as well as the final test. [s1]

This distinction matters when interpreting claims about domestic diagnostic capability. A test kit, an equipped laboratory, and a functioning national testing service represent different achievements. The Iranian experience provides evidence of coordinated assay assessment and laboratory support, rather than proof that every molecular test was equally accessible or accurate throughout the country. [s1][s2]

content.heading: How pandemic testing expanded
content.content:
An account published by Tabriz University of Medical Sciences describes an initial testing base at the Pasteur Institute of Iran and the National Influenza Laboratory. Expansion subsequently incorporated public-health laboratories, academic and research laboratories, and private laboratories meeting professional requirements. The authors identify the Iran COVID-19 Emergency Response Project, supported by the World Bank and WHO, as another contributor to capacity. [s2]

The equipment story is independently documented by WHO as a procurement partner. In October 2020, it reported delivering real-time PCR thermal cyclers intended for distribution to reference laboratories across multiple provinces. This confirms a specific equipment intervention; it does not establish subsequent utilization, uninterrupted reagent supplies, or the turnaround time experienced by patients. [s3]

The network therefore developed through institutional coordination as well as purchases. Research expertise could support clinical testing, but participation required standards and authorization rather than simply possession of a PCR machine. [s2]

content.heading: Quality assurance and the limits of the evidence
content.content:
The Pasteur Institute network account describes external quality assessment using unknown specimens sent to participating laboratories. Laboratories had to analyze the material and return results; failure triggered corrective action and reassessment. The national reference laboratory also participated in WHO assessments. These arrangements are evidence of a quality-control framework, although the article does not supply a public laboratory-by-laboratory performance history. [s1]

The same account describes developing a multiplex assay that could detect SARS-CoV-2 and influenza viruses together. This illustrates how an emergency testing platform could address overlapping respiratory infections. It should not be read as evidence that the assay remained universally available at the editorial cutoff. [s1]

For international readers, Iran’s pandemic laboratory response offers a concrete introduction to molecular diagnostics. A comprehensive account must additionally establish the contemporary position of inherited-disease testing, cancer diagnostics, reimbursement, regional access, and laboratory accreditation. The inspected evidence supports the infectious-disease case study more strongly than that wider national inventory. [s1][s2]

name: Genomics Research
description: Iranian population-genomics projects have developed reference resources for studying genetic variation and interpreting potential disease-associated variants. Iranome and a related population-genetics study demonstrate why Iranian diversity matters, while also showing the limits of treating a research cohort as a national clinical resource.

seo.title: Genomics Research and Iranome in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iranome, Iranian population-genetics research, and the limits of using reference databases to interpret human genetic variation.

content.heading: Why an Iranian reference resource matters
content.content:
Genomics research examines genetic variation across many genes or across the genome. For Iran, an important contribution has been building population-specific reference data. The original Iranome publication described whole-exome sequencing of 800 individuals from eight Iranian ethnic groups. Exome sequencing targets protein-coding regions; it should not be described as sequencing every participant’s entire genome. [s1]

The project addressed an interpretive problem: populations poorly represented in international reference resources may lack adequate local comparison data. Iranome was presented as a resource for understanding variation and supporting precision medicine, rather than as evidence that personalized treatment had already become routine. [s1]

A University of Toronto account describes collaboration involving researchers in Toronto and the Genetics Research Center at Iran’s University of Social Welfare and Rehabilitation Sciences. It explains the intended connection between variation databases and the interpretation of human disorders. Those aspirations distinguish the resource’s potential use from demonstrated improvements in patient outcomes. [s4]

content.heading: Different datasets answer different questions
content.content:
A related study published in PLOS Genetics examined genome-wide genotype data from 1,021 individuals after quality control, covering eleven ethnic groups. This was a population-genetics analysis, distinct from the original Iranome exome catalogue. Its findings emphasized both overlapping variation among several groups and substantial internal heterogeneity. [s2]

The practical implication concerns research design: sample selection and ancestry must be considered when investigating disease-associated variation. A finding in one sampled group cannot automatically characterize everyone in Iran. Nor do genetic similarities map neatly onto language or cultural identity; the study identified cases in which linguistic affiliation and genetic proximity differed. [s2]

These distinctions also discourage a misleading narrative of a single, uniform 'Iranian genome.' The studies provide reference observations from defined cohorts, with particular recruitment and analytical methods, rather than an exhaustive description of a national population. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Version history, consent, and access
content.content:
The live Iranome FAQ inspected for this page reports 1,202 sequenced samples. However, its statement about 'eight' ethnic groups accompanies a longer list of group names. Without a dated release history, that page cannot establish when the database changed or reconcile its current wording with the original publication. The published cohort is therefore the historical reference used here. [s3]

The PLOS study documents written informed consent and ethics approval. Its data-availability statement describes access restricted to population-genetic analyses through a data-access committee. Publication of aggregate results consequently should not be confused with unrestricted access to individual-level genetic data. [s2]

Iran’s documented contribution is a stronger empirical foundation for studying regional genetic diversity. Establishing clinical benefit requires additional evidence about how these resources are validated and used in diagnosis and care. [s1][s4]

name: Public Health
description: Public health in Iran combines community-based prevention, vaccination, chronic-disease programmes, environmental protection, and outbreak response. Its primary-care infrastructure provides an important platform, while differences in exposure, resources, and access require attention beyond national averages.

seo.title: Public Health in Iran: Prevention and Population Health | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s community health services, vaccination, chronic-disease prevention, environmental risks, and gaps in public-health evidence.

content.heading: Prevention close to home
content.content:
Public health addresses the conditions that shape health across populations, including prevention and early detection. Iran’s distinctive foundation is its community health network. UNICEF’s country brief describes rural health houses staffed by community health workers known as behvarzes, alongside urban workers called moraghebe-salamat. Their responsibilities include maternal and child health and the management of communicable and noncommunicable diseases. [s1]

This network was developed to improve access for disadvantaged communities and reduce rural–urban differences. Its importance is organizational: prevention can be delivered through a continuing local relationship rather than only during hospital treatment. Infrastructure nevertheless describes an opportunity to provide care, not a guarantee that every person receives the same service. [s1]

WHO’s country reporting recognizes continuing socioeconomic vulnerabilities and health inequities. It describes work with the Ministry of Health and Medical Education to integrate social determinants of health into primary care. Here, 'social determinants' means the circumstances affecting health beyond an individual consultation; the programme’s existence should be distinguished from demonstrated reductions in inequality. [s2]

content.heading: Vaccination requires surveillance as well as coverage
content.content:
Iran’s vaccination history includes verification of measles elimination by the end of 2019, as reported in a regional analysis published by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Elimination is an assessment of transmission within a defined setting, rather than a claim that imported infections can never occur. The analysis emphasizes maintaining both population immunity and high-quality surveillance. [s3]

Vaccination coverage and disease incidence answer different questions. Coverage estimates describe the proportion receiving a vaccine; surveillance seeks to identify infections and transmission. A high national estimate therefore does not remove the need to investigate local immunity gaps or suspected outbreaks. [s3]

The historical series below presents a single, explicitly identified WHO/UNICEF release. It preserves that release rather than combining historical values with newer numbers from another revision. It is useful for understanding the published record, but requires replacement with the latest comparable country series before this page is treated as current. [s4][s5]

content.title: Iran: estimated DTP3 coverage, 2012–2023, historical 2023 revision
content.interpretation: In this historical release, annual estimates remain between 98% and 99%. The small variation does not establish uniform local coverage; the source flags reporting and target-population concerns.

content.heading: Chronic disease changes the prevention agenda
content.content:
Noncommunicable diseases are conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, and chronic respiratory disease. Iran adapted WHO’s Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions into IraPEN, connecting prevention and care with the primary-care system. WHO’s historical account places IraPEN within the health transformation programme launched in 2014 and describes its connection with mental-health services. [s6]

This broadens prevention beyond vaccination. Risk assessment, identifying disease earlier, and maintaining appropriate follow-up become continuing responsibilities. However, an institutional description of medicines or programme design at one point in time cannot establish uninterrupted access or effective control in every district today. The historical WHO account is evidence of the programme’s approach, not a current audit of outcomes. [s6]

Public nutrition belongs within this agenda, but a national narrative needs evidence about food consumption, affordability, nutritional status, and differences between population groups. Those measures should remain distinct rather than being reduced to a single score. This page does not substitute an unverified national nutrition trend for that missing evidence.

content.heading: Healthy places and health across life
content.content:
Public health also extends beyond the health ministry. UNDP identifies urbanization, industrial emissions, and traffic congestion as contributors to Iran’s air-pollution challenge, particularly in major cities such as Tehran. This connects population health with transport, energy, industrial practice, and urban management. An environmental exposure should be assessed through its own measurements, rather than inferred from hospital capacity. [s7]

Regional circumstances also matter for infectious disease. WHO’s country reporting highlights malaria resurgence and a dengue outbreak in 2024, particularly in Sistan and Baluchestan. National averages alone cannot explain such geographically concentrated risks. The same reporting describes efforts to address health inequities through local institutions and primary care. [s2]

The branches of this public-health guide consequently cover disease prevention, public nutrition, environmental and occupational health, older people’s health, and maternal and child health. Each needs its own evidence about exposures, services, and outcomes. Iran’s community infrastructure provides a useful starting point; judging its contemporary performance requires current, geographically detailed information rather than assuming that programme design proves equal protection. [s1][s2]
